open-question.question: What is the exact one-sentence statement of the new identity (Cairn brings all the important questions up to be decided upfront, so long-running execution can be handed to agents confidently) that replaces "Milestone-driven development for your coding agent — any kind of work, one milestone at a time." under the title of the root README and the three host README templates?

Which noun do the pitch surfaces use for what Cairn is (for example "framework", "plugin", or "workflow"), given that the goal says "framework" while the manifests and CLAUDE.md say "plugin" and "workflow" today?
open-question.alternative: Every pitch surface uses "framework" as the noun for what Cairn is: the root README first screen and `## Why Cairn?`, the three host README templates, the three plugin manifest descriptions and the two marketplace descriptions, the opening sentence of `CLAUDE.md`'s `## What this repo is`, and the four GitHub repository descriptions. None of these surfaces calls Cairn a "plugin" or a "workflow". "Plugin" appears only in installation mechanics, such as `/plugin install` and "installed plugin directory". "Workflow" appears only where it names the milestone mechanism or a skill name, such as `init-milestone-base-workflow`. It matches the goal's own wording ("Cairn is the framework that…"). Every surface then gives the same one-noun identity, so the reframe reads as one deliberate change and doesn't collide with the "milestone-driven development workflow" phrasing it replaces. In the coding world "framework" usually means a code library you build an application on, so the noun can mislead a reader about what they install. It also contradicts the manifests, which are literally plugin manifests, and `CLAUDE.md`, whose reader is an editor of a plugin repository. Whether those two surfaces are pitch-bearing at all depends on how the sibling questions about manifest strings and `CLAUDE.md`'s opening settle.

"Framework" is the identity noun on every pitch surface. "Plugin" is kept as the noun for the delivery form on the surfaces that describe the installed artifact: the plugin and marketplace manifests, `CLAUDE.md`'s opening sentence, the host README templates and the distribution repository descriptions. The pattern is "a framework, shipped as a plugin for Claude Code, Antigravity, and Codex". "Workflow" stays only as the name of the milestone mechanism. It carries the goal's identity noun and stays literally accurate about what a user installs. That suits the artifact-facing surfaces (manifests, distribution repos, an editor reading `CLAUDE.md`) without letting "plugin" stand in for the identity. It uses two nouns, so some sentences have to carry both and get longer. That matters on the short surfaces: the one-liner, the marketplace string and the GitHub descriptions. It also rests on per-surface judgment about which surfaces are "artifact" ones, which the sibling questions on manifest strings, `CLAUDE.md` wording and distribution repository descriptions bear on.

Every pitch surface calls Cairn a "plugin", matching the current manifests and `CLAUDE.md` ("A plugin (`cairn`) for Claude Code, Antigravity, and Codex…"). This drops the goal's "framework" as loose phrasing rather than a commitment, and "workflow" drops out as an identity noun. It is the most accurate noun, since Cairn ships and installs as a plugin on all three hosts. It matches the existing manifests, `CLAUDE.md` and installation text, so the reframe changes only the claim and not the category, and it sets no expectation that Cairn is a code library. "Plugin" names the delivery vehicle rather than an identity, so it adds nothing to the decide-upfront pitch and reads as a minor add-on. It also departs from the goal's stated wording, which a reviewer may read as quietly narrowing the goal.

Every pitch surface calls Cairn a "workflow", for example "the workflow that brings the important questions up to be decided upfront…". This keeps the noun the manifests, root repository description and bootstrap block already use, minus the "milestone-driven development" qualifier. Neither "framework" nor "plugin" is used as the identity noun. It is the least disruptive noun. It is already the word on most surfaces and in this repository's own `## Milestone Workflow` block, and it describes a process the user follows rather than a library or an add-on. "Workflow" is the word most tied to the milestone-driven identity being retired, so the reframe can read as a reworded tagline rather than a new identity. It also departs from the goal's "framework" wording.

"Workflow" is the identity noun on every pitch surface, and "plugin" is kept as the delivery-form noun on the artifact-describing surfaces (manifests, `CLAUDE.md`'s opening, host README templates, distribution repository descriptions). This follows the pattern of today's `CLAUDE.md` sentence ("A plugin … that provides a … workflow"), with the qualifier replaced. "Framework" is not used. It is the closest to the current wording on every surface, so the change is limited to the identity claim. It is also accurate about both what the user follows and what they install. It keeps the word the old identity is built on and departs from the goal's "framework". Its two-noun sentences also run long on the short surfaces, and which surfaces count as artifact-describing depends on the sibling questions on manifest strings, `CLAUDE.md` wording and distribution repository descriptions.

The pitch surfaces adopt no category noun for Cairn. Each pitch sentence makes Cairn the subject of what it does, as in "Cairn brings the important questions up to be decided upfront…". "Plugin" stays only as a plain fact in installation and distribution text. "Framework" and "workflow" are not used as identity nouns. It avoids the misleading connotations of all three candidates and puts the claim itself in front. It also removes the inconsistency between surfaces by construction, since there is no noun left to disagree about. Some surfaces are conventionally noun-led, such as the GitHub description, the marketplace listing and `CLAUDE.md`'s "A plugin … that…" opener, and verb-led sentences can read as missing what the thing is. It also departs from the goal's explicit "the framework that…" phrasing.

No milestone-wide noun is fixed. Each surface keeps its current noun, or whatever its own rewrite picks, as that surface's wording is settled: "plugin" in `CLAUDE.md` and the distribution repositories, "workflow" in the manifests, and the README one-liner as worded there. Harmonizing the noun is not done in this milestone. It could be revisited in a later one if the mix proves confusing. It adds no cross-surface constraint, so each sibling wording decision (one-liner, manifest strings, `CLAUDE.md` opening, repository descriptions) is free to choose the most natural sentence for its own surface. The mix of "framework" in the goal and "plugin" and "workflow" elsewhere, which prompted this question, survives the reframe. A reader moving from the README to the marketplace listing or the GitHub description sees Cairn called different things, which weakens the "one identity" the goal asks for.

open-question.question: What happens to the bold tagline line "Mark the path from idea to shipped." that sits above the one-liner in the root README: is it kept as it is, replaced by a new tagline that expresses the decide-upfront identity, or removed so the one-liner stands alone?
open-question.alternative: The root README keeps the bold line "Mark the path from idea to shipped." exactly as it is, in its current place directly under `# Cairn` and above the one-liner. Only the one-liner below it carries the decide-upfront identity. The tagline is not reworded now or held for a later milestone; it simply stays. Nothing changes, and the reasons milestone 26 gave for keeping the line still hold. It costs no extra space on the first screen because it renders in the same paragraph as the one-liner. It is also the last visible trace of the trail-marker metaphor behind the name. Its wording never says "milestone-driven", so it does not contradict the new identity. The goal lists the tagline among the first-screen surfaces the reframe covers. "From idea to shipped" stresses the whole journey, not deciding before handing off, so the first line a reader sees still tells the old story while only the line under it tells the new one. Whether the two lines read as one message depends on the wording chosen by the sibling question on the identity one-liner.

The bold line is replaced by a new tagline in the same place. The new tagline keeps the cairn trail-marker image (marking a path) and points it at the decide-upfront identity: the path is marked before the walk, so the walk can be handed off. The one-liner stays below it as the plain statement. The first screen gets an identity-bearing lead line, and the link between the name and its meaning, which milestone 26 kept the tagline for, survives. The goal's listing of the tagline as a reframed surface is met, and the bold line and the one-liner tell one story. A new short line has to be written that does two jobs at once, the metaphor and the new identity. A forced or vague image weakens the first screen more than the current line does. It also overlaps the one-liner, so the two need to be worded together to avoid saying the same thing twice. This depends on the sibling questions on the one-liner's wording and on how strongly the claim is stated.

The bold line is replaced by a new tagline in the same place. The new tagline states the decide-upfront identity in plain words with no trail-marker image, for example a short slogan about deciding the important questions first and then handing off execution. The one-liner stays below it. It gives the clearest and most direct first line for the new identity. A reader learns what Cairn promises from the bold text alone, without decoding a metaphor. A literal line is also easier to keep in step with the manifests and repository descriptions. It drops the last visible explanation of the name Cairn, which milestone 26 deliberately kept. It also risks two lines that both state the identity literally, one bold and one plain, and so repeat each other. How much they overlap depends on the one-liner wording chosen by its sibling question, and the strength of the slogan depends on the claim-strength sibling question.

The bold line is deleted and nothing replaces it. The one-liner stands alone directly under `# Cairn` as the only statement of identity on the first screen. No tagline is added anywhere else. The first screen gets one unambiguous identity sentence, with no slogan beside it that could pull toward the old story or repeat the one-liner. It is also the smallest edit that leaves no surface on the first screen still pitching from-idea-to-shipped. It throws away the trail-marker metaphor and the benefit-first hook kept since milestone 1, leaving the name Cairn unexplained. The whole first impression then rests on one sentence, so its quality depends entirely on the wording chosen by the sibling question on the identity one-liner.

open-question.question: The goal states "all the important questions" at full strength as a guiding principle, while docs/design-claims.md records that no test yet measures it. Do the pitch surfaces state the claim as plain present-tense fact with no qualifier, or do they say somewhere that it is the principle Cairn is built toward?
open-question.alternative: No pitch surface carries a qualifier. The tagline, one-liner, `## Why Cairn?`, host README templates, plugin and marketplace manifest descriptions, the `CLAUDE.md` opening, and the GitHub repository descriptions all state the claim that Cairn brings all the important questions up to be decided upfront as plain present-tense fact. None of them adds a sentence or link that marks the claim as a principle Cairn is built toward or as unmeasured. `docs/design-claims.md` is not pointed to for this purpose and keeps whatever status it records. It gives the strongest and simplest reading of the new identity, and the wording is the same on every surface. Nothing hedges the first screen or the short description strings, where a qualifier costs the most attention. The pitch states as fact something the project's own `docs/design-claims.md` says no test measures: only claim 11's test runs, and milestone 38's re-run of the alternatives rules was recorded as unverified. A reader who reaches that page sees the gap with nothing in the pitch acknowledging it. The goal's own framing of the claim as "the guiding principle later milestones work toward" is also left unstated.

The pitch sentences stay plain present-tense fact on every surface, with no qualifying wording. The root README adds one explicit pointer, near the claim, to `docs/design-claims.md` as the place that records which claims are measured. The pointer itself says nothing about status, so the fact that "all the important questions" is a principle not yet measured is disclosed only one click away. No other surface carries the pointer or a qualifier. The pitch prose has no hedging, and the claim is still not left unbacked. Any reader who wants the evidence status finds it on the existing page, which already states that only claim 11's test is run. The disclosure is implicit, so a reader who does not follow the link never learns the claim is aspirational. How well it works depends on what the design-claims page says about claims 1 and 14 and on whether the README's design-principles block surfaces them. Both of those are owned by sibling questions (Design claims page scope, Design principles selection).

The short surfaces state the claim as plain present-tense fact: the one-liner, tagline, host README templates, manifest descriptions, the `CLAUDE.md` opening, and the GitHub repository descriptions. The root README's longer prose, its `## Why Cairn?` section, says once in plain words that bringing up all the important questions is the principle Cairn is built toward and that later milestones work toward it. It may also say that the claim is not yet measured. No short surface carries a qualifier. It matches the goal's own wording ("stated at full strength as the guiding principle later milestones work toward"). The claim is disclosed in the one place that has room for a sentence of context, and the one-liner and the character-limited description strings stay unhedged. Surfaces read without the root README carry the claim with no disclosure at all: the manifests, the marketplace listing, the repository descriptions, and the distribution repositories' host READMEs. Where the sentence sits, and how it reads beside the section's opening problem, depends on the shape of `## Why Cairn?`, which the Why Cairn argument sibling owns.

The pitch sentence carries its own framing as a design principle on every surface, for example "built so that…" or "designed to bring…" in place of a bare present-tense assertion. That framing reaches the one-liner and so the three host README templates that copy it verbatim. It also reaches the manifest and marketplace descriptions, the `CLAUDE.md` opening, and the GitHub repository descriptions. The root README may say more about the principle in its longer prose, but no surface states the claim as unqualified fact. No surface, including the ones read with no README context such as manifests, marketplace entries, and repository descriptions, claims more than the project's evidence supports. The pitch can never be quoted out of context as an unbacked factual claim. It weakens the identity at exactly the points where the goal wants it at full strength. Design-intent phrasing in the one-liner reads as hedging and makes the sentence longer. Whether it fits depends on the exact one-liner and on whether the manifests reuse that one-liner verbatim, which the Identity one-liner wording and Manifest description strings siblings own.

open-question.question: How does the root README's first-screen mermaid diagram change to express "decide upfront, then hand off execution"? What argument does the rewritten "## Why Cairn?" section of the root README make: which problem does it open with, and where in it do milestones (as the mechanism) and work-type neutrality (as a supporting point) appear?
open-question.alternative: The section opens with the problem of handing off long-running execution: an agent left to run for a long time hits questions nobody decided, and it either guesses quietly and builds on the guess, or stops and waits for a person. Either way you cannot walk away. A second paragraph presents milestones as the mechanism. Each milestone first brings its open questions up, has them answered with recorded decisions, and only then derives tasks that an agent can complete unattended. A third, closing paragraph makes work-type neutrality the supporting point: the workflow reads the project's environment from `CLAUDE.md`, so it fits any kind of work. This keeps today's three-paragraph structure but replaces the content of each paragraph. Each element of the goal gets its own paragraph in the order the goal gives them: identity problem, mechanism, supporting point. The opening problem is the exact pain that the decide-upfront identity and the headless chains in docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md answer, and today's paragraph never mentions it. The three paragraphs are about as long as today's section, so the new identity's argument is not made shorter or more pointed than the milestone-first version it replaces. The new opening also drops the familiar list of large-project failures, such as goal drift and an unbounded task list, which some readers recognise more easily than the failure of an agent run.

The section opens with the same handoff problem: a long-running agent meets questions nobody decided, and it either guesses or stops. One following paragraph gives the answer. It names milestones in a single clause as the unit in which questions are found and decided before any task is derived, and it ends with one sentence on work-type neutrality: the environment context in `CLAUDE.md` adapts the workflow to any kind of work. The section has two paragraphs, and neither milestones nor neutrality gets a paragraph of its own. The argument is the shortest and most focused option. Almost all of its weight goes on the problem and the decide-upfront answer, so milestones and neutrality are clearly secondary to the identity, which is what the goal's "mechanism" and "supporting point" ranking asks for. Milestones are reduced to one clause in the README's only argument section, so a reader learns how Cairn delivers on the claim only from the `## How it works` file list further down. Whether that lower section explains enough depends on whether it is reworded in this milestone, which the "Lower README sections scope" question decides.

The section keeps today's opening on the predictable ways large projects fail, but rewrites and reorders that list. Questions left undecided until the work is under way become the headline failure, and goal drift, an unbounded task list, and the missing line between working and done follow as its consequences. The section also adds the result: an agent cannot be trusted to run alone. The second paragraph is recast so that milestones are the mechanism for deciding questions upfront before execution is handed off, rather than "a structured, repeatable process". The third paragraph keeps work-type neutrality as the closing supporting point, much as it reads today. This is the smallest change. It keeps the familiar framing of large-project failures and the existing paragraph structure, and moves the emphasis onto undecided questions and handing off execution, so the section stays continuous with the docs and the earlier pitch. The opening problem is still about general project management, not about delegating to agents. The new identity therefore arrives as a reinterpretation of an old argument rather than as its premise, and it may read as the milestone-driven pitch with new emphasis instead of a clear reframe.

This option rejects the assumption that the section opens with a problem. It opens with the identity claim itself and its payoff: Cairn brings the important questions up to be decided before work starts, so long-running execution can be handed to agents with confidence. A second paragraph presents milestones as the mechanism that makes this true: questions are surfaced, alternatives are given, decisions are recorded, and only then are tasks derived and completed unattended. A closing paragraph gives work-type neutrality through `CLAUDE.md` as the supporting point. The failure the claim guards against appears at most as a contrast clause inside the first paragraph. The first sentence of the argument is the identity, which repeats and expands the first-screen one-liner. A reader who stops after one paragraph has the whole pitch, and the section never spends its opening on a problem the reader may not yet feel. Without a stated problem, the claim has nothing to argue against, so the section reads like a restated tagline rather than an argument for why Cairn is needed. It also stays very close to the one-liner, so the two risk repeating each other. How close they come depends on the wording the "Identity one-liner wording" question settles.

The section opens with the handoff problem (undecided questions make a long-running agent guess or stop) and follows it with one paragraph of payoff: decide the important questions upfront, then hand off execution, for any kind of work through the environment context in `CLAUDE.md`. The section never names milestones. The milestone mechanism is left entirely to `## How it works` and the docs. The argument shows the clearest break from the old identity, because it never uses the word that the previous pitch was built around. It is purely about the problem and the promise, so the milestone vocabulary cannot pull it back toward the milestone-driven reading. The goal says milestones are presented as the mechanism, and this option drops the mechanism from the README's only argument section. "Decide upfront" then reads as an aspiration with no visible means, which is risky for a claim that no test yet measures. Whether the mechanism appears anywhere on the pitch surfaces depends on how far `## How it works` is reworded, which the "Lower README sections scope" question owns.

The section opens with the handoff problem (undecided questions make a long-running agent guess or stop) and follows it with a paragraph that presents milestones as the mechanism for finding and deciding those questions before tasks are derived and executed unattended. The section ends there and leaves out work-type neutrality. The point appears elsewhere in the README, or nowhere. The argument is cut to identity plus mechanism with no secondary thread. That avoids a closing paragraph that changes the subject to project-type flexibility after the decide-upfront payoff has landed. The goal names work-type neutrality as a supporting point, and today's one-liner ("any kind of work") is the README's other carrier of it. If the rewritten one-liner also drops it, the point disappears from the README's first screen and argument altogether. That depends on the axis owned by the "Identity one-liner wording" question.
